Every autumn the festival returned to the valley, and every autumn it grew stranger. The first year it was booths and fiddles; the third year the fiddles were silent and only drums remained; the fifth year the drums gave way to a measured chant that the oldest villagers swore they remembered from their grandmothers' grandmothers. Nobody could say who lit the first brazier, but after that the bonfires never went out, ring after ring of them climbing the hillside like a second constellation. A cartographer came to map the valley and stayed for the bonfires. He filled three notebooks with distances and angles, took the festival's measurements with the care of a man recording a cathedral, and left the fourth notebook blank, telling the innkeeper that some structures resisted mapping. The children believed the bonfires kept the winter wolves at bay, and the wolves, for their part, gave the fires a wide berth, drifting through the orchards like smoke with eyes. On the final night the whole valley stood silent while the hill burned, and in the morning the bonfires were ash, the booths were gone, and the cartographer's notebooks sat on the innkeeper's shelf, four of them now blank. The festival returns every autumn, and every autumn the valley asks fewer questions and listens longer.
